title: Business Workflows, State, Lifecycle & Invariants
status: Blueprint frozen for lesson planning — lessons not implemented
engineeringQuestion: What must remain correct regardless of the eventual architecture?
premise: Correctness must be specified before deployment topology. The first implementation begins as one real, testable Spring Boot deployable; diagrams and simulators are explanatory models, not implementation evidence.

chapters.title: Business reality, responsibility and authority
chapters.why: Discover who is allowed to decide what, why each actor acts, and how a business request becomes an authoritative fact without assuming a service boundary.

lessons.title: Actors, goals, responsibilities and capabilities
lessons.question: Who participates in an order and whose goal does each operation serve?
outcomes: Construct a role/capability matrix for Customer, Restaurant, Payment Provider, Operations and Delivery.
Identify commercial decisions versus software responsibilities and external authorities.
prerequisites: General application APIs and HTTP are assumed; no DDD vocabulary required.
scope: Actors and stakeholders; incentives; customer experience; restaurant capacity; payment settlement exposure; responsibilities; business goals; authorization decisions; human versus automated actors.
mechanisms: Walk through one customer purchase, restaurant rejection and provider reversal; identify who may initiate, approve and observe each decision.
visuals: Editable actor-capability map with authority edges and contradictory-control warnings.
Timeline of a single order from menu selection through fulfillment.
examples: Customer cancels after restaurant accepts; merchant refuses out-of-stock item; provider does not confirm card authorization.
lessons.project: C: document actors, responsibility boundaries, business scenarios; no Java changes before commands and use cases are understood.
experiments: Scenario-based role mapping and counterexample review; baseline evidence is a written requirements model.
diagnosis: Symptom: two parties believe they own cancellation; distinguish missing business policy from a network fault.
mastery: Derive roles from an unfamiliar workflow, recognize ambiguous authority, and explain to nontechnical stakeholders.
transfer: 60-second actor explanation; Staff review challenges whether Restaurant or Payment owns an order's payment status.

lessons.title: Business scenarios and use-case discovery
lessons.question: Which end-to-end user outcomes must a runnable platform support first?
outcomes: Write precise success, rejection and exceptional paths for place, accept, reject, cancel, pay, refund, prepare and complete.
Choose one real vertical slice with explicit acceptance criteria and minimal dependencies.
scope: Business capabilities; use-case boundaries; input intent; actor permissions; preconditions; postconditions; negative outcomes; bounded MVP scope; observation vs authority.
mechanisms: Trace customer place-order intent into application decision and visible result; compare restaurant acceptance/rejection and payment result as separate concerns.
visuals: Choose-an-actor use-case journey with alternate branches.
Sequence lanes: Customer → Platform → Restaurant → Payment Provider.
examples: Place then restaurant rejects; restaurant accepts but payment fails; customer cancels while kitchen begins preparation.
lessons.project: A: initialize Java 21 root Maven and single Spring Boot deployable with initial place-order HTTP vertical slice, domain/application separation, in-memory adapter, unit tests and CI. No future microservices.
experiments: Execute Maven root verify; positive/negative order placement, duplicate request test design; capture exact toolchain and commit SHA.
diagnosis: A 2xx HTTP response is not automatically a completed business transaction; inspect use-case postcondition.
mastery: Explain runnable slice, source/test paths and why not to introduce Kafka or PostgreSQL in this lesson.
transfer: Defend MVP scope and why a single deployable is the simpler architecture.

lessons.title: Commands, decisions, facts and events
lessons.question: What separates an intention to change state from proof that it changed?
outcomes: Classify commands, rejected decisions and committed business facts without confusing emitted messages with authority.
Design command contracts that identify actor, target, expected state and business meaning.
scope: Commands vs facts/events; decision outcomes; negative facts; events as historical claims; side-effect intentions; acknowledgement; idempotency key concepts without distributed protocol yet.
mechanisms: Trace PlaceOrder → decision → OrderPlaced; AcceptOrder → decision → OrderAccepted; rejected attempts do not imply a successful domain fact.
visuals: Command/event sorting board; execution sequence from HTTP request to decision and persisted fact.
Alternative timeline distinguishing intent from actual effect.
examples: Repeated PlaceOrder with same user intent; refund requested but not yet confirmed; merchant rejection before payment capture.
lessons.project: A: add application commands and explicit outcomes/events for validated first workflows; tests verify rejected commands cannot emit success facts.
experiments: Unit tests for legal command outcomes, event ordering within local execution and rejection semantics.
diagnosis: Customer sees 'success' but no persisted fact; discriminate API interpretation from application failure.
mastery: Given a log of messages, identify which facts are authoritative and which are only requests.
transfer: Explain command/event distinction at junior, Senior and Staff depth without claiming events imply event sourcing.

lessons.title: Business identity and authoritative state
lessons.question: Which identities are stable and which component is entitled to determine a fact?
outcomes: Distinguish OrderId, PaymentAttemptId, RestaurantId, CustomerId and correlation/request IDs.
Specify authoritative versus derived state and identify cross-model references without forcing contexts or services prematurely.
scope: Identity continuity; natural/surrogate references; generated identifiers; authority; state version; immutable history; aliasing; request/trace/business identifiers; ownership mapping.
mechanisms: Compare changing order status with recording payment provider outcome; a UI read model does not become authoritative by showing a status.
visuals: Identity/ownership graph highlighting authoritative source and projection readers.
Change-an-identity exercise showing duplicate/alias impacts.
examples: Two payment attempts for one order; same restaurant name under different merchant IDs; repeated callbacks.
lessons.project: A: introduce typed stable business IDs and clearly owned mutable state to the single application; local verification for identity continuity.
experiments: Entity identity tests across updates; repeated request does not silently create new OrderId when semantic rules prohibit it.
diagnosis: A status read disagrees with a provider receipt; list alternate hypotheses before selecting the source of truth.
mastery: Defend authority and identity map; recognize ambiguous derived views.
transfer: Staff challenge: who may assert 'payment completed' if provider response is delayed?

lessons.title: A complete Food Ordering workflow story
lessons.question: How do responsibilities compose into a customer-visible business outcome?
outcomes: Trace Order, Restaurant and Payment participation including rejection, cancellation, refund, preparation and completion.
Identify business outcomes, policies and unsettled assumptions before implementation.
scope: End-to-end scenario storyboarding; business collaboration; state vs observed messages; partial completion; receipt and refund implications; delivery handoff boundaries.
mechanisms: Build success and failure narrative; highlight where an unimplemented external provider must be simulated and where irreversible kitchen or financial effects begin.
visuals: Swimlane journey with branching paths and actor-controlled choices.
State/authority overlay for every milestone.
examples: Paid and rejected; accepted then cancelled; preparation already started; refund requested but not confirmed.
lessons.project: C: establish process map and decision backlog; no additional code required for narrative work.
experiments: Narrative walkthrough evidence + unanswered policy register.
diagnosis: Diagnose conflicting customer and merchant screens with authority and timeline evidence.
mastery: Trace every business fact to an actor and policy; identify at least three unresolved constraints.
transfer: Explain a partial customer journey to an engineering manager and a nontechnical stakeholder.

chapters.title: Lifecycle semantics and decision mechanisms
chapters.why: Turn the business narrative into explicit states, legal decisions and before/after conditions, while preserving the distinction between a workflow and its participating state machines.

lessons.title: Workflows versus state machines
lessons.question: Why is a workflow not a single state diagram?
outcomes: Model independent lifecycles for Order, PaymentAttempt and RestaurantDecision.
Derive how a multi-actor workflow coordinates those lifecycles without claiming atomicity across them.
scope: Workflow phases; explicit states; transition functions; separate state authority; state explosion; cross-lifecycle predicates.
mechanisms: Step through distinct order, payment and restaurant lifecycle states; demonstrate a workflow can progress while one participant remains pending.
visuals: Side-by-side lifecycle graphs; click a transition to reveal actor, guard and fact.
Workflow swimlane overlay.
examples: Payment authorized while merchant decision pending; restaurant rejects while refund pending.
lessons.project: A: introduce explicit lifecycle types/transitions in domain modules of the single deployable; no cross-service calls.
experiments: Transition table-driven tests with valid and invalid paths for each lifecycle.
diagnosis: Incorrectly model 'REFUNDED' as an Order status and lose independent payment history; show diagnosis.
mastery: Explain why Order aggregate state cannot represent every participant's state; identify missing context without creating services.
transfer: Defend a model split without confusing module with deployable.

lessons.title: Guards, preconditions and postconditions
lessons.question: What makes a requested transition legal in a particular state?
outcomes: Write total transition decision tables including guard failures and expected effects.
Separate required preconditions from side effects and ensure illegal commands leave state unchanged.
scope: Transition guard; business authorization; precondition; postcondition; state preservation; failure result; side-effect-free rejection; illegal transitions.
mechanisms: Trace AcceptOrder: current=PLACED and eligible restaurant actor; mark checks, commit point and resulting fact.
visuals: Transition-table inspector with selectable current state/actor/command.
Rule explanation panel showing checked guards and no-op rejection.
examples: Accept already rejected order; mark preparing before acceptance; complete before preparation.
lessons.project: A: implement guarded transition methods and application outcomes; preserve state on forbidden operations.
experiments: Parameterized positive/negative transition tests; assert no success fact and no mutation on rejection.
diagnosis: Suspected illegal transition: compare business guard, stale state and adapter mapping mistakes.
mastery: Derive tests from model rather than from controller behavior alone.
transfer: Staff reviewer adds one exception policy mid-explanation; revise guards coherently.

lessons.title: Terminal, reversible and irreversible business effects
lessons.question: When does 'undo' mean reversal, and when is compensation required?
outcomes: Classify terminal states and reversible operations in Order, Restaurant and Payment flows.
Explain why provider refund and kitchen preparation cannot be undone by restoring old fields.
scope: Terminal state; correction; reversal; compensation; irreversible external effect; lifecycle closure; audit trail; human intervention.
mechanisms: Contrast canceling an unpaid draft with refunding a completed charge; compare kitchen preparation with metadata rollback.
visuals: Undo-versus-compensate decision tree; before/after business facts timeline.
examples: Refund after successful capture; cancelled order after ingredients consumed; notification already sent.
lessons.project: C: document policy and missing provider API assumptions; do not claim real refunds without provider integration.
experiments: Policy examples and counterexamples; trace attempted reversal and required compensating action.
diagnosis: A previous order state is restored in DB but provider still charged: identify irreversibility and recovery work.
mastery: Independently decide reversal versus compensation in a foreign domain.
transfer: Explain financial compensation carefully without introducing Saga prematurely.

lessons.title: Ordering, payment and restaurant lifecycle composition
lessons.question: How do independent decisions constrain a shared business journey?
outcomes: Define concrete ordering/payment/accept/reject/cancel/refund/prep/complete policies and exceptions.
Distinguish confirmed payment facts from requested or simulated provider outcomes.
scope: Cross-lifecycle guards; payment attempt state; restaurant acceptance authority; cancellation window; preparation and completion; partial completion; refund initiation/outcome.
mechanisms: Walk an accepted-but-unpaid case and rejected-but-paid case without hiding unresolved money state.
visuals: Three synchronized state machines with highlighted guard dependencies.
Sequence view switching happy path and failure path.
examples: Payment after cancellation; merchant reject after capture; customer cancel while preparation starts.
lessons.project: A: add deterministic local payment-provider simulation interface and restaurant decisions to real application workflow; record that provider is simulated.
experiments: Integrated application tests for payment/restaurant/order transitions and recorded business outcomes; no fake external payment claim.
diagnosis: Customer reports charge but merchant sees rejection; reconstruct state and provider-simulation assumptions.
mastery: Specify policy choices and identify which require later strong persistence or distributed consistency.
transfer: Explain to Staff how failures will change once these calls become remote.

lessons.title: Workflow boundaries and collaboration without microservices
lessons.question: Which interactions belong in one deployable now, and why?
outcomes: Design in-process boundaries between Order, Restaurant and Payment responsibilities.
Identify potential future ownership seams without creating microservices and their network uncertainty.
scope: Business collaboration; application service orchestration; semantic modules; in-process calls; local atomicity assumptions; future remote boundary candidates.
mechanisms: Compare single-process call sequence with proposed remote calls; enumerate latency, failure and duplicated effects as hypothetical new forces.
visuals: Architecture dependency explorer, single-app baseline versus future extraction as a hypothesis.
In-process sequence diagram with commit boundaries.
examples: A restaurant decision API is called twice; compare local handling with conceptual remote duplicate.
lessons.project: C: record modular architecture rationale/ADR; make only changes required to enforce already-discovered source responsibilities.
experiments: Architectural dependency tests if code structure warrants; evidence-backed no-split decision.
diagnosis: A shared model creates coupling; distinguish package/design smell from a need for a network boundary.
mastery: Defend non-distribution as an active choice and list measurement triggers for reconsideration.
transfer: Staff interview: why not launch OrderService and PaymentService on day one?

chapters.title: Invariants, concurrency, duplicates and consistency windows
chapters.why: Make correctness claims falsifiable by constructing stale, duplicated and competing decision sequences and separating fragile teaching models from verified runtime guarantees.

lessons.title: Invariant versus validation versus database constraint
lessons.question: What must remain true even when input validation passes?
outcomes: Derive domain invariants across order/payment/restaurant facts.
Distinguish request validation, domain invariants and local persistence constraints with counterexamples.
scope: Validation; domain invariant; database constraint; immutable business rule; concurrent write risk; atomicity; scope of enforcement.
mechanisms: Show 'valid JSON' and valid amount yet illegal payment-after-cancel; compare app guard and database unique constraint.
visuals: Invariant builder with scope and enforcement-layer toggles.
Three-column rule-to-evidence matrix.
examples: Two accepted cancellations; negative amount caught by validation; duplicate payment success despite valid schema.
lessons.project: A: assert critical business invariants in domain/application logic and tests; defer PostgreSQL constraints until Cluster 1.2 when DB-backed guarantees can be observed.
experiments: Counterexample-based tests and documented non-guarantees; simulated validation is never called DB protection.
diagnosis: Unexpected duplicate payment: distinguish input validation bug from missing state/commit guard.
mastery: State each invariant formally, its enforcement boundary and unsolved concurrency assumptions.
transfer: Defend why @NotNull alone does not protect payment correctness.

lessons.title: Repeated commands and duplicate business effects
lessons.question: Why can a command be received twice and what should remain unchanged?
outcomes: Define duplicate-request semantics separately for place, accept, pay, cancel and refund.
Identify when repeating a command should return previous result, reject, or create a new attempt.
scope: Command identity; duplicate intent; business effect; repeated HTTP request; idempotency as semantic property; same key/different payload; incomplete outcome.
mechanisms: Replay one request before/after state update and classify effects; distinguish an additional PaymentAttempt from accidental duplicate capture.
visuals: Duplicate-command ledger and before/after effect counters.
Retry timeline with command-ID and business-ID labels.
examples: Customer double-click; provider callback repeated; repeated refund initiation.
lessons.project: A: implement locally deterministic repeat-command handling for selected workflows and unit tests; state that this does not prove distributed exactly-once semantics.
experiments: Repeat-command tests, conflict payload tests and reset/replay evidence.
diagnosis: Two receipts appear: determine whether two commands, two successful state changes or duplicated view/event were observed.
mastery: Document replay outcome and safeguards for each command type.
transfer: Staff challenges idempotency key lifetime and payload mismatch; name what remains undecided until Phase IV.

lessons.title: Cancellation-versus-acceptance interleaving
lessons.question: Can two separately valid decisions both succeed incorrectly?
outcomes: Predict concurrent command outcomes given identical observed state.
Demonstrate why check-then-write without atomic guard can violate exclusive business outcomes.
scope: Racing reads; stale snapshot; linearization/commit point intuition; lost updates; guard-and-write atomicity; synchronization limitations.
mechanisms: Interleave Customer.Cancel and Restaurant.Accept at read/check/write stages; compare unsafe blind write with single atomic compare-and-update.
visuals: Required simulator: actor lanes, interleaving mode, safe/unsafe toggle, step-by-step timeline, both-success invariant alarm.
examples: Cancellation and acceptance both observe PLACED, both claim success; last-write-wins DB state conceals business contradiction.
lessons.project: B: preserve fragile race as reproducible test/experiment; introduce local concurrency control only where a measurable reproduced violation requires it.
experiments: Concurrent deterministic tests/barriers, model counterexample, observed vs assumed notes; no cross-process correctness claim.
diagnosis: One customer sees cancellation, restaurant sees accepted: construct competing causal hypotheses and a discriminating test.
mastery: Independently identify race window, specify minimal guard, explain why local synchronization alone may not solve multi-process writes.
transfer: Staff interviewer introduces two instances and asks what guarantee changes.

lessons.title: Payment-after-cancellation and modification-after-payment
lessons.question: What changes when a delayed financial outcome arrives after business state moved?
outcomes: Distinguish payment initiation, authorization, capture and recorded confirmation in a simulated provider.
Design policy for order mutation once financial commitment or merchant acceptance changes.
scope: Delayed outcomes; order modification guards; payment-after-cancel policy; refund-needed state; external side-effect uncertainty.
mechanisms: Record attempt, mark order cancelled, then deliver success outcome; trace unresolved financial obligation without reverting cancellation.
visuals: Delayed payment outcome timeline with business versus provider state.
Modification guard matrix by order/payment state.
examples: Pay succeeds after cancel; amount changes after authorization; refund requested but pending.
lessons.project: B: implement controlled provider-simulator delay scenarios and tests, not real payment integration or Saga/Outbox.
experiments: Tests for immutable confirmed amounts, refund obligation, late outcome, state/history consistency.
diagnosis: Customer 'charged after cancel': inspect provider outcome, system fact, callback time and missing evidence.
mastery: State what is guaranteed locally and what will need asynchronous coordination later.
transfer: Explain to nontechnical stakeholder why cancellation does not imply immediate financial reversal.

lessons.title: Stale decisions and versioned state
lessons.question: How can valid business checks become invalid before they commit?
outcomes: Describe TOCTOU decision windows and distinguish stale read from stale authority.
Derive version-based guards and show where a version check must be atomic with mutation.
scope: Time-of-check/time-of-use; snapshot; version; compare-and-set; lost update; transaction isolation intuition; auditability.
mechanisms: Two clients use Order version 4; one commits version 5, the other tries version 4; contrast optimistic conflict with blind overwrite.
visuals: Versioned state timeline with two concurrent readers and conflict result.
Concurrency warning overlay.
examples: Accepted order later cancelled from stale snapshot; repeated payment attempt with stale amount.
lessons.project: B: show reproducible stale-state test and architecture note; DB-level optimistic locking deferred until Cluster 1.2 real PostgreSQL integration.
experiments: Barrier-driven conflict tests and explicit 'simulated vs locally observed vs database-guaranteed' classification.
diagnosis: Lost update observed: isolate stale reads, commit ordering and read-model freshness as alternate causes.
mastery: Specify exact required atomic comparison for a promised guarantee.
transfer: Staff challenge asks whether an in-memory version field suffices across replicas.

lessons.title: Atomicity, consistency boundaries and unknown commit outcomes
lessons.question: What state changes must succeed or fail together, and what cannot be made atomic by one in-memory method?
outcomes: Identify locally coherent transitions and cross-participant decisions that cannot be presumed atomic.
State guarantees, assumptions and non-guarantees around persistence, concurrency and external provider effects.
scope: Atomic transition; all-or-nothing local update; external effects; consistency boundary; crash window; durable versus transient state; uncertainty after timeout.
mechanisms: Mark business state plus local fact and explore crash before/after each step; compare conceptual external provider uncertainty.
visuals: Commit-window storyboard with application, adapter and provider states.
Guarantee ledger: observed/assumed/not guaranteed.
examples: Crash after provider success but before local record; timeout with unknown provider status; partial in-memory update.
lessons.project: C: document consistency boundary and minimal application test gaps; no premature transaction framework, Saga or outbox.
experiments: Thought experiment and tests only where runtime conditions can be controlled; unknown outcomes labeled not guaranteed.
diagnosis: Distinguish process crash, partial business failure and HTTP loss; choose evidence for each.
mastery: Draw scope of local atomic guarantee accurately and list unresolved distributed windows.
transfer: Defend why a local @Transactional annotation cannot atomically commit a remote provider effect.

chapters.title: Verification, diagnosis, architectural defense and transfer
chapters.why: Turn requirements and fragile-state examples into testable evidence, incident reasoning and independent Staff-level design communication.

lessons.title: Correctness test design and evidence hierarchy
lessons.question: Which tests would falsify a proposed business invariant?
outcomes: Construct transition, command, property, negative, concurrency and integration test matrices.
Keep claims limited to executed environments and distinguish tests from database or production guarantees.
scope: Test pyramid; state-based and transition tests; invariants; concurrency barriers; reproducibility; evidence labels; experiment controls; CI gates.
mechanisms: Derive tests for legal/illegal decisions, repeated commands and races; align observed outcomes with precise invariant claims.
visuals: Interactive test matrix coverage grid; one-click counterexample explanation.
Evidence badge toggles distinguishing observed and hypothetical.
examples: Unit tests pass but same API request race fails; CI green for unit suite but integration not run.
lessons.project: A: ensure Maven root verify and relevant application tests execute; add any missing tests only where justified and capture real outputs.
experiments: Test command manifest, exit codes, environment, evidence links and negative cases; no claim of PASS if not executed.
diagnosis: A green test badge masks missing failure scenario: identify scope hole rather than declaring full correctness.
mastery: Create verification plan and accurately label strength/limitations of evidence.
transfer: Staff challenge: which test is discriminating and which is merely a happy-path example?

lessons.title: Production-oriented failure diagnosis
lessons.question: How can a failure report be translated into competing hypotheses and discriminating evidence?
outcomes: Reconstruct symptom, scope, chronology and likely causal windows.
Avoid treating one timeout/log/event as proof of root cause.
scope: Incident symptom; affected users; timeline; logs/identifiers; competing hypotheses; discriminating test; causal chain; mitigation; validation.
mechanisms: Investigate duplicate payment and conflicting order status as separate incidents; choose what telemetry would disambiguate them.
visuals: Interactive diagnostic evidence board: choose among hypotheses and reveal clues.
Timeline builder with uncertain ordering.
examples: Customer cancelled but restaurant prepared; duplicate provider charge versus duplicated display fact.
lessons.project: B: isolate reproducible failure scenarios and capture logs/tests locally; advanced distributed traces deferred.
experiments: Observed reproduction record, log correlation limits and explicit next-step diagnostic tests.
diagnosis: Hypothesis: event delivered twice; alternate: command processed twice; choose evidence distinguishing them.
mastery: Explain a credible causal chain and a safe mitigation, including what remains unproven.
transfer: Adapt incident briefing for engineer, manager and nontechnical stakeholder.

lessons.title: Simpler alternatives, architectural decisions and deferment
lessons.question: When is doing less the better architecture?
outcomes: Compare minimal guarded local workflow with imagined microservice/Kafka/Saga alternatives.
Write evidence-based ADRs with trade-offs, risks and reconsideration triggers.
scope: Simplicity vs distributed complexity; quality attributes; migration cost; decision reversibility; ADR; removal trigger; known fragility.
mechanisms: Compare synchronous in-process decisions to remote ownership; enumerate new failure windows, operational burden and legitimate future split forces.
visuals: Architecture alternatives slider: same business need, cost/failure/ownership tradeoffs.
ADR evidence decision tree.
examples: Overengineered Kafka for a local state update; insufficient ownership clarity; harmful shared database.
lessons.project: C: record topology ADR; any project code change must have an existing demonstrated force rather than being a decoration.
experiments: Decision record cites observed/assumed evidence and contains explicit revisit conditions.
diagnosis: A design change is suggested because of a transient error; separate signal from architectural force.
mastery: Defend retaining one deployable in Phase I and explain when the decision should change.
transfer: Staff interview: 10× load, team halved, payment provider unstable; revise recommendation without dogma.

lessons.title: Communication, unfamiliar-domain transfer and cluster exit gate
lessons.question: Can you independently derive, validate and defend correctness constraints in a different business domain?
outcomes: Explain business rule, mechanism and trade-off at increasing abstraction levels.
Transfer invariants/authority/reversal reasoning to reservations, inventory or ledger-like operations.
scope: Synthesis of actors, intents, facts, authority, lifecycle, guards, terminality, invariants, concurrency, duplicate/stale operations, atomicity, evidence and defense.
mechanisms: New scenario arrives with missing facts; reconstruct lifecycle, write invariants, predict race, choose tests and defend simple design.
visuals: Timed design canvas with revealing constraints; competency rubric; dependency/retrieval links to 1.2, 1.3, 1.4 and Phases III–IX.
examples: Hotel room booked twice; inventory oversold; payment reversal requested after ledger posting.
lessons.project: C: freeze verified Cluster 1.1 checkpoint state and handoff; app build remains meaningful only if tests actually executed.
experiments: Mastery gate: explain/implement/test/diagnose/defend; evidence-index with actual SHAs, limits and deferred mechanisms.
diagnosis: Interviewer supplies ambiguous duplicate booking; enumerate hypotheses and specify evidence plan.
mastery: Independently produce invariant table, trade-off analysis and readable Staff-level explanation.
transfer: Adapt explanations for backend engineer, Staff/Principal reviewer, engineering manager and stakeholder; assess English clarity separately.

actors: Payment provider (controlled simulator in first implementation)
guarantees: Business rule requires that accepted and cancelled outcomes not both be reported successfully for the same version of an order.
A documented rule is not proof that the in-memory or DB implementation enforces it under concurrency.
openPolicies: May a customer cancel after Restaurant accepts? Initially assume no, then compare alternative window policies.
Does payment occur before or after restaurant acceptance? Model both and choose one for the first implementation.
Can a restaurant partially accept order items? Defer until core lifecycle established.
When is a refund economically final? Only an actual provider confirmation may establish it.
Who handles delivery failure after preparation? Record as open later workflow dependency.

prerequisites: Actors → capabilities → use cases → commands → facts → identities → lifecycles → guards → invariants → conflicts → tests
causality: Customer intent → authorized command → decision/guard → state mutation → authoritative fact → observed outcome
failures: Two read PLACED → both pass guard → interleaving writes → contradictory success → repair by atomic guard and verified evidence
project: Requirements → minimal Spring Boot vertical slice → expanded local lifecycle → race experiment → verified invariant tests → ADR
evidence: Prediction → controlled variables → executed test → observed transition / invariant result → interpretation / uncertainty → design decision

labs.title: Interleaving Race Explorer
labs.model: Single-order, two-actor deterministic state machine: Cancel and Accept; choose atomic check/update vs unsafe check-then-write; vary arrival order; show both-success contradiction.
labs.limitations: Educational deterministic model; does not reproduce JPA, network or multi-process transactions.
labs.proof: Pure transition unit tests + later Java concurrency harness

labs.title: Lifecycle Composer
labs.model: Separate Order, PaymentAttempt, RestaurantDecision lifecycles with cross-state predicates.
labs.limitations: Lifecycle policy is provisional until business validation.

labs.title: Authority Map
labs.model: Actors and source-of-truth graph for critical business facts.
labs.limitations: Organizational choices are business requirements, not code guarantees.

labs.title: Duplicate Command Ledger
labs.model: Replay command identities over order/payment attempts and classify duplicate effect policy.
labs.limitations: Local semantic demo, not distributed exactly-once delivery.

labs.title: Diagnosis Caseboard
labs.model: Competing hypotheses for late payment, duplicate provider receipt or conflicting acceptance.
labs.limitations: Synthetic case; observed project evidence linked separately after experiments.

applicationPlan.change: Produce actors, scenario matrix and authority map without making a Java repo commit.
Initialize Java 21 Maven root, single Spring Boot deployable, minimal PlaceOrder HTTP flow, in-memory repository, unit tests, CI; first verification checkpoint.
Explicit command/fact/outcome types and stable business IDs; preserve simple structure and unit tests.
Scenario inventory, unresolved business-policy register and complete actor journey.
Lifecycle and transition guards for Order, PaymentAttempt and RestaurantDecision; table-driven tests.
Document reversibility and external compensation limitations; no fake provider effects.
Add local, explicitly simulated payment provider and restaurant decisions with testable policies.
Record no-premature-split ADR with measured/revisit criteria.
Enforce invariants, repeat-command handling for selected operations, negative tests.
Reproducible concurrency, duplicate and late-payment experiments; preserve fragile baseline, no unjustified infrastructure.
Document atomicity boundaries and unresolved durable/remote uncertainty; defer DB-backed guarantees to 1.2.
Close specific test gaps, run root Maven verification and inspect CI evidence.
Incident hypothesis evidence exercises linked to executed failure harnesses where available.
ADR, design defense, cross-domain mastery and handoff; freeze verified checkpoint SHAs.

caveats: No actual Java tests are run in Phase 0 because the platform is intentionally not yet implemented.
Simulation results are not runtime observations.

masteryGate: Derive business actor/authority and use cases independently.
Provide a falsifiable lifecycle and invariant table for Order, Restaurant and Payment.
Predict outcomes under duplicate, cancellation race, late payment and stale-state cases.
Reproduce a relevant test or explain precisely why execution evidence is unavailable.
Distinguish documented rule, implemented guard, observed result and environment-bound guarantee.
Diagnose at least one failure using multiple hypotheses and a discriminating test.
Defend one simpler alternative and one overengineering failure to a Staff reviewer.
Transfer correctness reasoning to a different domain, without copying solution shapes.

forwardDependencies.why: Aggregate and transaction boundaries from invariants; real PostgreSQL and optimistic concurrency.
Separate semantic ownership and translate ambiguous models.
Remote execution creates uncertainty around previously local decisions.
Retries, duplicate effects and ambiguous outcomes become distributed.
Distributed data ownership, consistency and freshness.
Multi-authority workflows, compensation and reliable propagation.

deferred: Multiple Spring Boot services by default
Kafka, Redis, Outbox, Saga, CQRS, Event Sourcing
Production-wide concurrency claims from in-memory tests
